strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks: its principal contribution is UniEM-3M rather than the incremental Cellpose-inspired architecture. On that basis, the scale—5,091 high-resolution micrographs and approximately 2.99 million instance masks—is potentially valuable for materials-oriented computer vision.
The collection targets an important, underserved domain and includes unusually crowded scenes, broad object-scale variation, structured descriptions, and both segmentation and generation components.
The human-in-the-loop annotation platform, iterative refinement, peer inspection, expert audit, and versioned comments indicate substantial engineering and annotation effort.

The experiments cover several representative segmentation families. UniEM-Net obtains strong reported results, particularly on the dense subset, and the synthetic-data experiments suggest potentially useful augmentation benefits.
The manuscript is generally understandable and includes dataset statistics, implementation details, qualitative comparisons, prompts, and clear visual examples.
weaknesses: The release policy substantially undermines the dataset contribution: only an unspecified subset of the images will be public, while the complete benchmark and its annotations apparently remain unavailable. The paper does not state the subset size, selection procedure, licenses, access terms, or whether the official test set and evaluation infrastructure will be released. Consequently, the headline results on the complete UniEM-3M may not be independently reproducible.

There is a serious possible test-contamination issue. The abstract and introduction state that the diffusion model is trained on the entire collection, while its generated images are subsequently used for segmentation training and evaluation of augmentation. If “entire” includes the 963-image test partition, this gives the training pipeline access to the test distribution and potentially individual test images. The paper must establish that all generative-model training, token learning, annotation-model training, and data selection exclude the test set.

Dataset provenance and split construction are inadequately documented. The data mix academic collaborations, automated web crawling, and Aversa et al.; source-wise counts, licensing or redistribution rights, specimen/instrument identities, and the train/test grouping rule are absent. Perceptual-hash deduplication alone does not prevent different views or crops of the same specimen from crossing splits. This is especially problematic for scientific images and may inflate performance.

Annotation quality is described procedurally but not measured. There is no blinded audit sample, inter-annotator agreement, boundary accuracy, error rate, or comparison of pseudo-labels before and after correction. Most masks originate from iterative model predictions refined by volunteers, so describing all roughly three million instances simply as expert-annotated overstates the demonstrated supervision quality. The circular use of synthetic data and segmentation models during dataset construction also requires a frozen, independently annotated test set.

The synthetic segmentation experiments are not reproducible because the manuscript never explains how instance masks are obtained for SDXL-generated images. If masks are produced by the same segmentation model, Tables 3 and Figure 6 may largely measure self-training rather than the claimed quality and utility of generated data.

The benchmark protocol is not sufficiently rigorous or fair. UniEM-Net is trained for 180,000 iterations, whereas competitors are described as trained for 72 epochs with default settings; several methods receive different backbones and parameter budgets; and many baselines are omitted entirely from the dense evaluation. There are no multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, ablations of UniEM-Net's components, compute/runtime measurements, or evaluation on an external dataset.

The reported “mAP@0.5” is not standard mAP: the paper defines a single-threshold matching score TP/(TP+FP+FN), averaged per image, without describing confidence ranking or a precision-recall integral. Calling this standard mAP is misleading, and evaluation only at IoU 0.5 can conceal poor boundary precision. PQ is likewise reported only at 0.5 without sufficient implementation detail.

The structured textual modality is weakly validated. Material identity, microscopy type, and Z-axis layering may not be reliably inferable from pixels alone, yet GPT/Gemini outputs are evaluated only through mutual cross-checking and unspecified expert resolution. No annotation-accuracy sample, per-attribute agreement, multimodal benchmark, or quantitative prompt-controllability study is presented.

Claims of universality and multimodality are overstated: 90.9% of the data are SEM images, the category distribution is long-tailed, and no cross-instrument, cross-material, TEM-specific, or external-domain generalization results are provided. The roughly three-million-instance headline also obscures the comparatively modest number of independent images.

The generation evidence is limited. FID and average DINO cosine similarity are insufficient to establish scientific validity, the real-data FID of 28.06 against the stated training distribution is unexplained, t-SNE overlap is not reliable evidence of distribution matching, and the allegedly novel out-of-distribution structures receive no physical or expert validation. Overall, the resource could be impactful, but incomplete release, possible test leakage, unclear synthetic labels, and absent quantitative annotation validation prevent a convincing benchmark contribution in its current form.

strengths: Assessed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: approximately 5,091 electron micrographs and 2.99 million instance masks would constitute a useful resource if its quality, provenance, and accessibility were established.
The collection targets genuinely difficult computer-vision conditions, including dense scenes, irregular morphology, large scale variation, and images containing thousands of instances.

The paper evaluates several detection-, center-, and flow-based segmentation families and provides useful qualitative comparisons. The result that flow-based approaches are better suited to dense microstructures is plausible and potentially valuable.
The annotation platform, staged human review, structured descriptions, and synthetic-data augmentation form an ambitious end-to-end data-engineering effort.
weaknesses: The main contribution is not actually made reproducible: only an unspecified subset of UniEM-3M will be public, while the complete dataset underlies the benchmark, reported results, and released diffusion model. A generator is not a substitute for access to the benchmark data or labels.

Dataset provenance and governance are seriously underspecified. A substantial portion is obtained through automated web crawling, but the paper gives no source breakdown, licensing analysis, redistribution permissions, or treatment of copyrighted, confidential, and identifying microscope metadata. The claim that the diffusion model is a privacy-preserving surrogate is unsupported by memorization or extraction tests.

Annotation reliability is asserted rather than measured. Most masks originate from iterative pseudo-labeling followed by volunteer correction, yet there is no independently annotated evaluation subset, inter-annotator agreement, boundary-quality study, audit sample size, error rate, or comparison with expert-only masks. These omissions are consequential for a dataset paper claiming nearly three million reliable instances.

The train/test split is described only as an image-level split. There is no grouping by specimen, acquisition session, laboratory, source, material, or near-duplicate series, leaving substantial risk that closely related micrographs occur on both sides. Perceptual-hash deduplication alone does not establish leakage-free evaluation, and no validation split is documented.

The segmentation benchmark is not sufficiently controlled. Several methods are evaluated only on the sparse subset, so the paper cannot empirically conclude that they fail on dense images; no runtime, memory, or failure statistics are reported. Methods also use different backbones, codebases, schedules, and training budgets, while uncertainty across runs is absent.

UniEM-Net is too incompletely specified to support reproduction or its large performance gain. The energy function, modified Euler integration, targets, network heads, losses, post-processing, and differences from Cellpose/CellViT are not formally described. There are no ablations isolating the claimed local geometry, skeleton, global analysis, SAM backbone, or synthetic data.

The synthetic-data experiment omits a critical detail: the manuscript does not explain how instance masks are obtained for diffusion-generated images used to train the segmentation model. Without the label-generation and quality-control procedure, Table 3 cannot be interpreted or reproduced.

The generative evaluation is weak for the claims made. FID with natural-image Inception features and a mean DINO cosine score do not establish scientific fidelity, text-attribute correctness, compositional control, non-memorization, or physically plausible out-of-distribution generation. The t-SNE visualization is not quantitative evidence, no expert evaluation is reported, and the comparison setup and sample sizes are unclear.

Reported synthetic-pretraining gains over SA-1B appear small and are given without repeated trials, error bars, matched compute details, or statistical tests. Likewise, only IoU-0.5 segmentation metrics are reported, with no threshold-averaged AP, boundary accuracy, counting error, or downstream particle-size/distribution measurements relevant to materials characterization.

The term “universal” is overstated: 90.9% of the data are SEM images, multiple categories are highly imbalanced, and no cross-instrument, cross-laboratory, cross-material, or external-dataset generalization experiment is presented. Overall, the scale and application are promising, but access, provenance, label validity, split integrity, and reproducibility concerns prevent a convincing benchmark contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, under-served computer-vision problem: dense instance segmentation in heterogeneous materials electron micrographs. The proposed Datasets/Benchmarks contribution is potentially valuable even though its main significance does not rest on algorithmic novelty.

UniEM-3M is substantial in annotation scale: 5,091 high-resolution images and approximately 2.99 million instance masks, with over 30% of images reportedly containing more than 500 instances. The inclusion of structured attributes and both SEM and TEM imagery broadens its potential utility.

The human-in-the-loop annotation system is thoughtfully designed for unusually dense scenes, including model-assisted initialization, magnetic-lasso tooling, two peer inspections, expert audit, versioning, and localized review comments.

The benchmark spans detection-, center-, and flow-based segmentation families. Results expose meaningful failure modes of natural-image methods and show strong performance for UniEM-Net, especially on the sparse subset (0.824 mAP@0.5 versus 0.605 for Cellpose-SAM).

The synthetic-data experiments suggest practical value: generated-only training approaches the performance of smaller real datasets, while combining 30K generated images with 4K real images improves mAP@0.5 from 0.800 to 0.807. Synthetic pretraining also consistently improves the reported data-efficiency curve.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and supported by useful dataset statistics and qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The principal benchmark is not reproducible from the promised release: only an unspecified subset of UniEM-3M will be public, while evaluation is performed on the complete private collection. The paper must state exactly which images, masks, descriptions, splits, code, checkpoints, and licenses will be released and ideally provide a fully public benchmark test protocol.

Dataset provenance and legal/ethical status are insufficiently documented. A substantial portion is obtained through automated web crawling, but source attribution, licenses, consent or terms-of-use compliance, removal procedures, and per-image provenance are not described. Cropping watermarks or manufacturer metadata does not resolve copyright concerns.

Split integrity is unclear. Perceptual-hash deduplication alone does not prevent near-duplicate fields of view or images from the same specimen, acquisition session, paper, or video from entering both training and test sets. Grouped splitting by source and specimen, leakage analysis, and an external-dataset evaluation are needed to support generalization claims.

Annotation quality is described procedurally but not measured. There is no inter-annotator agreement, expert re-annotation study, boundary-quality statistic, error rate, or clear cross-morphology definition of an “instance.” Because pseudo-labels initialize annotation, the benchmark may also inherit model-specific biases that favor related flow-based methods.

The synthetic-data pipeline omits a crucial detail: SDXL is trained on image-text pairs, yet the 30K generated images are used for instance-segmentation training without explaining how their pixel-level instance masks are obtained or validated. This makes the augmentation and pretraining results difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The claim that the released diffusion model is a privacy-preserving proxy for the full dataset is not supported by differential-privacy training, membership-inference tests, nearest-neighbor or memorization analysis, or sensitive-attribute leakage evaluation. FID, feature cosine similarity, and t-SNE overlap do not establish privacy or faithful distributional substitution.

UniEM-Net is presented at a high level and appears closely derived from Cellpose-style flow prediction with a SAM-ViT backbone. The exact architectural changes, energy construction, modified Euler integration, losses, and post-processing are not specified sufficiently, and there are no ablations isolating the claimed local/global components. Its dense-set advantage over Cellpose-SAM is also small in PQ (0.703 versus 0.700).

Benchmark fairness needs stronger justification. UniEM-Net is reported as trained for 180K iterations, whereas competitors use 72 epochs and largely default configurations; several baselines are excluded entirely from dense evaluation. Runtime, peak memory, input-resolution handling, variability across seeds, and confidence intervals are absent despite efficiency being part of the motivation.

The generative evaluation is under-specified: sample counts, train/test separation, FID protocol, and the aggregation used for DINO cosine “Style” similarity are missing. Calling attribute-recombined samples out-of-distribution is unsupported without demonstrating that combinations are absent from training data or evaluating attribute adherence with experts.

Overall, the dataset could have high impact, but the unspecified partial release and unresolved reproducibility, provenance, leakage, annotation-quality, and synthetic-labeling issues prevent a sufficiently convincing benchmark contribution in its current form. These concerns lead to a slight preference for rejection despite the paper's strong potential.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General because its central contribution is EM3M. At the reported scale—5,091 electron micrographs and 2,985,660 instance masks spanning diverse materials, morphologies, instruments, and densities—the resource could fill an important gap in materials-oriented computer vision.

The dataset targets a genuinely difficult and practically relevant regime: images can contain thousands of instances, instance areas span several orders of magnitude, and boundaries are often low-contrast, overlapping, or highly textured. The paper provides useful statistics and explicitly identifies unresolved challenges such as boundary precision, fibrous structures, and within-image scale variation.

The human-in-the-loop annotation workflow is more careful than simple model-generated labeling: pseudo-labels receive peer review and expert validation, while a stratified 300-image subset is independently annotated by three annotators. Reporting agreement at multiple pipeline stages is valuable evidence that review improves the labels.

The benchmark covers several major instance-segmentation paradigms and reports both sparse-subset and full-dataset results for bottom-up methods. The strong performance of flow-based representations in crowded micrographs is a useful empirical finding, regardless of the limited algorithmic novelty of UniAIMS.

The synthetic-data experiments provide promising downstream evidence: performance increases with generated-data volume, generated pretraining improves over SA-1B pretraining, and combining 30K generated images with real data improves mAP from 0.800 to 0.809. External evaluation on EMPS and Okunev also offers preliminary evidence of transfer.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. It appropriately acknowledges that AP/PQ@0.5 is lenient and reports the substantial drop of UniAIMS to PQ@0.9=0.340 rather than presenting the benchmark as solved.
weaknesses: The release and provenance story is inadequate for a dataset contribution. The manuscript states that the dataset, model, and demo are publicly available, but the corresponding footnotes contain no usable links. More importantly, approximately 10% of the images are web-crawled, yet the paper gives no source list, licenses, redistribution permissions, attribution policy, or removal procedure. Release rights for the 84% obtained through collaborations are also not documented. These omissions materially limit reproducibility and safe reuse.

The random 4,128/963 train/test split is risky for microscopy data pooled from over 60 institutions. Images from the same specimen, acquisition session, publication, instrument, or web source could appear in both splits; perceptual-hash deduplication does not exclude correlated fields of view. A source/specimen-grouped split and leakage audit are needed before the reported generalization numbers can be trusted.

The annotation ontology is underspecified. The paper does not define consistently what constitutes an instance across particles, grains, fibers, pores, aggregates, overlapping structures, and ambiguous boundaries. For the 300-image validation subset, it is also unclear how the three annotations are reconciled into the stated ground truth, how images are stratified, or how uncertainty varies by morphology and density. Thus the reported average KA/PQ values do not justify the strong claim that expert-level quality is guaranteed across nearly three million masks.

The structured text annotations are much less convincingly validated than the masks. Several attributes—material identity, microscopy type, surface texture, and apparent Z-axis layering—may not be reliably inferable from pixels alone. The descriptions originate from GPT/Gemini and undergo unspecified human review, with no per-attribute agreement, expert accuracy, controlled vocabulary, or held-out audit. Calling the attributes 'disentangled' or 'quasi-orthogonal' is unsupported and conflicts with the paper's acknowledgment of observed attribute correlations.

The central synthetic-augmentation experiment is not reproducible because the paper never explains how instance masks are obtained for the 5K–30K diffusion-generated images. This is consequential: a text-to-image model generates images but not aligned instance labels, and the validity of the reported segmentation gains depends directly on how those labels were produced and quality-controlled. SDXL/LoRA training details such as rank, optimization schedule, resolution, sampling settings, and token construction are also largely absent.

The generation evaluation is insufficient for claims of controllability and replacement of real data. FID against spatially augmented real images is an unconventional 'real' reference, and sample counts and feature-extraction details are missing. Mean DINO cosine similarity and t-SNE overlap do not establish diversity, prompt/attribute faithfulness, physical plausibility, or absence of training-image memorization. No expert evaluation, nearest-neighbor analysis, precision/recall metric, or quantitative attribute-control test is provided.

The benchmark does not substantiate the claim that detection- and query-based models fail under extreme density because those methods are evaluated only on images with fewer than 100 instances. Keeping default 100-detection/query limits measures out-of-the-box configurations, not the paradigms' attainable performance. The memory plot appears strongly dependent on the data-loading representation, and no tuned limits, tiled inference, density-controlled curves, or full-set results are supplied.

The UniAIMS comparison is confounded. Cellpose is trained on one GPU with 256×256 inputs, whereas UniAIMS uses distributed training and larger-resolution inputs; UniAIMS simultaneously changes the backbone, size model, augmentation, flow computation, and training infrastructure. There is no component-wise ablation, multiple-seed uncertainty, matched-resolution comparison, or runtime/memory table. Consequently, the large gain from 0.711 to 0.800 full-set mAP cannot be attributed to the proposed adaptations, and the practical value of the CUDA implementation is not quantified.

Overall, the dataset's scale and potential impact make the decision close, but the missing release/provenance information, leakage-prone split, underspecified annotation ontology, unexplained synthetic labels, and confounded benchmark leave the scientific case just short of acceptance.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the paper is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks: its main value is EM3M rather than the modest UniAIMS modifications. On that basis, 5,091 micrographs and nearly three million instance masks could constitute a useful resource for dense microstructure analysis. The dataset appears substantially larger and more instance-dense than the cited public electron-micrograph segmentation datasets, and it covers varied morphologies, scales, materials, and microscopy settings.

The human-in-the-loop annotation process includes peer review, expert auditing, versioning, and an independently re-annotated subset. Reporting inter-annotator agreement is a welcome attempt to quantify label quality.

The benchmark covers several segmentation paradigms, and the results identify a practically relevant challenge: conventional proposal- and query-based systems do not readily accommodate thousands of instances per image.

The authors acknowledge important remaining problems, including weak performance at strict overlap thresholds, ambiguous boundaries, fibrous structures, scale variation, and a gap from human agreement.
External-dataset evaluation and experiments varying real and synthetic training volume are useful directions for assessing practical utility.
weaknesses: Dataset provenance and release legality are insufficiently documented. Approximately 10% of the data is web-crawled, yet the manuscript gives no source inventory, licensing analysis, redistribution permission, or attribution protocol. The claim that EM3M consists of raw experimental micrographs is also difficult to reconcile with web-sourced images and reused public data. These omissions are consequential for a dataset paper whose main contribution is public release.

The random image-level train/test split is not adequately protected against leakage. Electron-microscopy collections commonly contain multiple crops, magnifications, or acquisitions from the same specimen or session. Perceptual-hash deduplication alone does not establish independence, and no specimen-, study-, institution-, or acquisition-group split is reported. Consequently, the main benchmark may measure interpolation across closely related images rather than generalization.

The annotation target is underspecified. The paper does not provide sufficiently precise rules for what constitutes an instance across particles, grains, fibers, aggregates, overlapping structures, cropped objects, and ambiguous boundaries. The reported validation also lacks essential details: stratification of the 300-image subset, annotator qualifications, blinding, instance-matching protocol, uncertainty, and per-morphology results. Pixel-level Krippendorff's alpha can obscure instance-splitting and merging errors, while the relationship between the re-annotations, the stated ground truth, and the three pipeline-stage evaluations is unclear.

Several textual attributes are not reliably inferable from pixels alone, including material identity, microscopy modality in some cases, and especially Z-axis layering. Although outputs receive human review, the paper reports no per-attribute accuracy or agreement, correction rate, metadata verification, or expert protocol. Thus, the claimed high-fidelity multimodal annotations are not convincingly validated.

The central benchmark comparison is not fair or comprehensive. Detection- and query-based methods are evaluated only on a less challenging subset with fewer than 100 instances, so the paper does not actually measure their claimed failure on the full dense benchmark. Different methods also use materially different resolutions, backbones, implementations, schedules, and hardware constraints; notably, Cellpose is trained at 256x256 on one GPU while UniAIMS uses distributed training, larger inputs, a ViT backbone, and other engineering changes. The large performance difference therefore cannot be attributed to the proposed adaptations.

Evaluation is too narrow for scientific microstructure measurement. The reported 'mAP' is a microscopy-specific per-image F1-like quantity at IoU 0.5 rather than conventional average precision, and the principal results rely on lenient AP/PQ at 0.5. The admitted drop from PQ 0.704 to 0.340 at the stricter criterion indicates that boundary and shape fidelity—the quantities relevant to materials characterization—remain weak. No boundary, size-distribution, morphology-measurement, or counting errors are evaluated.

The synthetic-data experiment has a major reproducibility and validity gap: the manuscript never clearly explains how instance masks are obtained for the 5K–30K generated images. If they are pseudo-labels from the segmentation model, the evaluation risks circular self-training and cannot establish that the diffusion model creates correctly annotated examples. Training schedules and compute are also not controlled when comparing real-only and real-plus-generated data, and the final gain from augmentation is only 0.009 mAP without seeds or uncertainty estimates.

The generative evaluation does not support the strong claims. FID with ImageNet features is acknowledged to be unsuitable, but is still used; treating FID between real images and geometric augmentations as a fidelity reference is not a validated calibration. A vaguely defined DINO cosine 'Style' score and t-SNE overlap do not demonstrate prompt adherence, diversity, absence of memorization, or physical plausibility. There is no expert study or nearest-neighbor analysis, yet the paper claims synthetic data could replace real data.

Reproducibility remains inadequate: no validation split or model-selection protocol is described; results lack repeated runs, uncertainty, and resource-normalized comparisons; key thresholds and post-processing settings are missing; and the claimed public dataset, model, and demo links are blank in the manuscript, preventing verification of files, licenses, code, annotations, and documentation.

UniAIMS itself offers limited originality, consisting mainly of removing Cellpose's size model, adding large-scale jitter, distributed training, CUDA preprocessing, and a stronger backbone. Such engineering could be valuable as a dataset baseline, but the experiments do not isolate the contribution of each change through ablations. Overall, the potentially valuable dataset is outweighed by unresolved provenance, leakage, annotation-validity, benchmark-fairness, and synthetic-label concerns.

strengths: Best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. EM3M is potentially valuable: 5,091 electron micrographs, 2,985,660 instance masks, structured descriptions, and unusually dense scenes address a genuine resource gap in materials-oriented computer vision. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/30a982c09b3a4da480933954d1113b19/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The annotation workflow is stronger than typical model-assisted curation: seed annotations, iterative pseudo-label refinement, two peer inspections, expert audit, versioning, and an independently re-annotated 300-image subset. Reported inter-annotator agreement and progressive PQ/KA improvements provide useful evidence of mask quality.

The benchmark covers detection-, query-, polygon-, embedding-, and flow-based paradigms. Results identify a practically important failure regime—hundreds or thousands of instances per image—and show that bottom-up representations scale better than standard proposal/query systems.

The synthetic-data experiments go beyond visual examples: increasing generated-data volume improves segmentation, 30K synthetic plus 4K real images raises mAP/PQ from 0.800/0.704 to 0.809/0.707, and synthetic pretraining helps across real-data scales.

UniAIMS is appropriately presented as an engineered baseline rather than a fundamentally new architecture. Its scale-robust augmentation, accelerated flow construction, higher-resolution distributed training, and strong full-set performance make it useful for future comparison.

The paper is generally clear, visually informative, and commendably candid about remaining failures: PQ falls from 0.704 at IoU 0.5 to 0.340 at IoU 0.9, fibrous structures remain difficult, and model performance trails human agreement.
weaknesses: The random image-level split is a major benchmark risk. Images from the same institution, experiment, specimen, acquisition session, or closely related material batch may enter both training and test sets; perceptual-hash deduplication does not prevent this semantic leakage. A source/specimen-grouped split and near-duplicate audit are needed to substantiate generalization.

Data provenance and release governance are insufficiently documented, especially for the 10% obtained by web crawling and the 84% supplied through collaborations. The paper should specify licenses or permissions, redistribution rights, source records, excluded sensitive metadata, and whether every image and annotation can actually be released.

The structured text modality receives little direct validation. Material identity and microscopy type can be impossible to infer reliably from pixels alone, yet Gemini/GPT predictions are described as high-fidelity without attribute-wise expert accuracy or agreement statistics. Controlled generation is likewise shown qualitatively without measuring prompt-attribute adherence.

The synthetic-data pipeline is not reproducible from the description: it is unclear how instance masks are obtained for generated images, whether pseudo-labels are used, and how their errors are controlled. Results lack multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and matched-compute controls; the claimed ability of synthetic data to replace real data is therefore too strong.

The benchmark is partly confounded. Top-down/query methods are evaluated only on the <100-instance subset, so their alleged failure under extreme density is inferred mainly from architectural limits and a Mask R-CNN memory study rather than measured task performance. UniAIMS also benefits from 1024-pixel, multi-GPU training and implementation changes while official Cellpose uses 256-pixel single-GPU training, weakening attribution of the large gain to the proposed adaptations.

No validation split or checkpoint-selection protocol is described despite training models “until full convergence.” The reported “mAP” is actually a microscopy-style per-image TP/(TP+FP+FN) score rather than conventional mean average precision, and results are mostly limited to IoU 0.5; boundary-sensitive metrics and stricter-threshold comparisons should be central for quantitative microstructure analysis.

Several presentation inconsistencies merit correction: the supplement says SEM exceeds 90% although its chart reports 84.9%, and the paper alternates between Cellpose code/backbone descriptions that make the exact implementation difficult to reconstruct. Complete configurations, preprocessing, label-generation code, and fixed splits are needed for a dependable public benchmark.
